# **Monitoring, Reporting and Verification procedures for soil health: Current landscape, stakeholder dynamics and future pathways**

Authors: Camille Imbert^1^, Antonio Bispo^2^, Sophia Götzinger^3^, Peter
Hoebe^4^, Taru Sandén^3^, Sambit Shome^1^, Lucile Rabeau^5^ and Kilian
Walz^6^

Affiliations:

^1^ Leibniz-Centre for Agricultural Landscape Research (ZALF),
Eberswalder Str. 84, D-15384 Müncheberg, Germany

^2^ INRAE Info&Sols, 2163, avenue de la Pomme de Pin, CS 40001 Ardon,
45075 Orléans cedex 2, France

^3^ Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety -- AGES, Institute for
Sustainable Plant Production, Department for Soil Health and Plant
Nutrition, Spargelfeldstraße 191, A-1220 Wien, Austria

^4^ Earthwatch Europe, 102-104 St Aldates, Oxford, OX1 1BT, United
Kingdom

^5^ Independent researcher, 24 cité des fleurs, 75017 Paris, France

^6^ Commonland Foundation, Kraanspoor 26, 1033 SE Amsterdam, Netherlands
\

Correspondence to: Camille Imbert camille.imbert@zalf.de

Keywords: Monitoring Reporting Verification (MRV), Soil health, Carbon
market, Literature review, Web scrapping, Artificial Intelligence
browser, Transparency, Monitoring accuracy


# Abstract

To counteract green washing, the effects of the activities that lead to
an intended outcome should be quantified and monitored in a
scientifically robust way and results should be transparently reported
and verified. With this objective, Monitoring, Reporting and
Verification (MRV) procedures were developed and studied in the context
of soil carbon credits. However, no broader overview, including other
aspects of soils, exists to date. The objective of this study was to
fill this gap of knowledge by gathering, describing and classifying the
MRV procedures including soil parameters, across the world. As the term
MRV seems to be sparsely used by scientists, we combined three
methodologies to collect information about MRV procedures: the classical
use of scientific article database, web scraping and Artificial
Intelligence browsers. We found 96 MRV procedures and partial
information was available. Most of the available MRV procedures were
applied on a local scale, in agricultural areas, responding to the
methodological requirements of voluntary carbon markets standards, which
illustrates the hegemony of carbon markets in the soil MRV context.
Results were mainly gathered in a classical report and result-based
verified. We classified the MRV procedures into six groups. Group 1 was
only characterized by the lack of information and thus reflected the
main limitation of our study. The five other groups addressed different
stakeholders. Four of them targeted stakeholders of the agricultural
sector and the last one project developers for peatlands and wetland
restoration. The two largest groups demonstrated different strategies:
more accurate monitoring and verification methodologies or cheaper ones.
We also highlighted the lack of transparency from companies offering MRV
procedures. In complement, we developed a decision tool to help future
users of MRV procedures to navigate our dataset and select the most
adequate MRV procedure, adapted to their context. The next steps are 1)
to strengthen the collaboration between scientists and MRV providers and
to 2) understand how to transition from carbon-focused MRV procedures to
more holistic, soil health-focused MRV procedures.

# Short summary

We classified 96 Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) procedures
including soil parameters. They were applied on a local scale, in
agriculture, focusing on soil carbon, using a classical report and
result-based verification. The six groups differed by available
information, targeted stakeholders, monitoring and verification
strategies. We also developed a decision tool. Next steps are to
strengthen scientists-MRV providers collaboration and to transition to
soil health MRV procedures.

# 1. Introduction

Numerous measures to preserve or restore soil health are applied by
stakeholders such as adopting agro-ecological practices, de-sealing or
planting trees (Altieri et al., 2015; Bárcena et al., 2014; Vieillard et
al., 2024). Healthy soils correspond to soils that are in good chemical,
biological, and physical conditions, and which can therefore provide
ecosystem services vital to humans and the environment, such as a safe,
nutritious and sufficient food, biomass, clean water, nutrient cycling,
carbon storage, and a habitat for biodiversity (Directive 2025/2360,
2025, Vasquez et al., 2025). To create an incentive for land managers to
preserve and restore soil health, few instruments are currently
available. On a global level, voluntary carbon markets have been
evolving as one of the major market-based instruments allowing to
generate and trade credits as certified units that help to finance the
adoption of more sustainable agricultural practices (Batjes et al.,
2024, Regulation EU 2024/3012, 2024). A carbon credit is a certificate
that represents one ton of CO2-equivalent and is the common trading unit
on carbon markets
([**https://www.offsetguide.org/understanding-carbon-offsets/what-is-a-carbon-offset/**](https://www.offsetguide.org/understanding-carbon-offsets/what-is-a-carbon-offset/)).
However, in several cases, carbon offsetting projects were deemed to
under deliver on the expected climate mitigation outcomes leading to
numerous situations for which actions to preserve the environment (like
the mitigation of climate change) did not attain what the stakeholder
had claimed (Trouwloon et al., 2023). These scandals led to allegations
of green washing and discredited the effectiveness of carbon credits as
means to achieve climate mitigation (Probst et al., 2024; Schreefel et
al., 2023; Trencher et al., 2024). A prominent example is the
non-commensurate use of carbon credits to achieve greenhouse gas
reductions beyond offsetting solely residual emissions as is prescribed
in voluntary best-practice guidance (Trouwloon et al., 2023).

To counteract green washing, the effects of the activities that lead to
an intended outcome should be quantified and monitored in a
scientifically robust way and results should be transparently reported
and verified. This is the main purpose of Monitoring, Reporting and
Verification (MRV) procedures (Smith et al., 2020). They are transparent
and accurate frameworks giving indications in the way to assess the
impact of an action on an object. Regarding soils, the main objective of
the MRV procedures is to demonstrate the effect of land management
(mainly, e.g. moving to agro-ecological practices or reforestation), on
soil parameters (such as organic matter content or biodiversity).
Moreover, MRV procedures not centered on soils but on other topics such
as forest conservation can include the assessment of soil parameters.

The term MRV seems to be sparsely known by soil stakeholders except to
those active on the carbon markets (Batjes et al. 2024). In the soil
scientific community, this term has been promoted by the two recent EU
projects BENCHMARKS and MARVIC (<https://soilhealthbenchmarks.eu/,>
<https://www.project-marvic.eu/> ). Until now, scientists mainly
described carbon-focused MRV procedures and no classification targeting
a larger spectrum of purposes exists (Batjes et al. 2024).

Thus, there is a need to go beyond carbon and identify all the MRV
procedures including soil parameters. Indeed, MRV procedures can be
applied in all the contexts dealing with soils. The main involved
stakeholders are land managers as farmers, foresters or public
administration but also scientists, NGOs and companies are concerned
because they encourage practices enhancing soil health. Within soil
monitoring, biological, physical and chemical soil parameters can be
assessed via sampling, proximal (site images) or remote sensing,
modelling or several of these methodologies combined (Batjes et al.,
2024). Land management information, collected with questionnaires and
provided by land managers, can also be used as proxy for soil parameters
(Batjes et al., 2024). Result uncertainty is computed with probabilistic
methods (Markov chain Monte Carlo and Bayesian inference), a sensitivity
analysis or basic quantile distribution (with the representation and/or
consideration of the quantiles in the result interpretation (Ceschia et
al., 2025). Data are compared to reference values to determine if the
implemented action is beneficial to soil health. Matson et al., 2024
describes four methodologies for computing these reference values 1)
fixed value i.e. a static value based on the literrature, 2) reference
value i.e.a static value from a reference site, mainly natural areas, 3)
data distribution i.e. based on regional data, or 4) relative change
i.e. a comparison to the data previously collected on the same site.
Results are gathered in a document or entered on an online platform
(Andries et al. 2021). The verification could take two forms:
result-based i.e. doubling soil measurements with the same or a
different methodology than for the monitoring step, or action-based i.e.
the implementation of the actions is verified during a site visit, a
second soil sampling, by remote sensing or with a phone application
(Andries et al., 2021, Batjes et al., 2024). The auditor can be part of
the organization implementing the soil monitoring or act as an
independent entity.

\
In this study, we reviewed and classified the adoption of MRV procedures
for assessing soil health and, assessed whether they are used beyond the
context of carbon markets. We also identified the involved stakeholders,
as well as the soil management practices. We proposed a decision support
tool to help future users to select the right MRV procedure,
corresponding to their context.

As we suspected that few scientific articles would be written on the
topic of soil MRV procedures, we decided to combine three review
methods: the traditional literature review using a database of
scientific articles and the recent ones web scraping and AI browsers
(Perplexity and Elicit). While traditional literature review has been
the common method for any academic researcher, web scraping allowed for
accessing grey literature from websites in a more systematic manner
(Sayles et al., 2022). Most recently, Artificial Intelligence has
emerged providing a wide array of search capabilities and in particular,
browsers as Perplexity and Elicit trained for the scientists.

Our findings are very relevant for future stakeholders that wish to
develop or simply implement MRV procedures for assessing their soil
health status and will enable to identify existing approaches or build
upon them, with a view to adapting existing practices to their needs and
context.

# 2. Materials and methods

## 2.1. Data search

As MRV procedures on soils seem to be not well studied, we decided to
use a very broad search string: **Monitor\* AND Report\* AND Verif\* AND
MRV AND soil\***.

We used it for the three methods we combined to scientific articles and
websites presenting MRV procedures: a search on the database of
scientific articles Scopus, webscraping and the use of Artificial
Intelligence browsers Elicit
([**https://elicit.com/**](https://elicit.com/)) and Perplexity
([**https://www.perplexity.ai/**](https://www.perplexity.ai/)). The
search was done in Scopus in March 2025 and includes article titles,
abstracts and keywords. It resulted in 18 articles (primary studies,
reviews and book chapters). We recorded the name of the first author,
the title, the publication year, the DOI and the type of document i.e.if
it was a primary study, an editorial article or a review. Then, we
developed a web scraping script using Python 3.9.7 and Selenium web
driver (Appendix 2,
[**https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/**](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/)).
We ran the script to scrap the first 20 pages on Google Search Engine
Results Page (SERP). We manually handled reCAPTCHA images. As results
provided by Google varied according to the country location, the date
and the IP address, we decided to run the script during Autumn 2025,
from different countries and different computers in Europe (See Code and
data availability). We recorded the URL link, webpage title and URL
domain in a database for further analysis. We used the Artificial
Intelligence browsers Perplexity and Elicit in December 2025 with the
following prompt: "*I would like to investigate existing Monitoring,
Reporting and Verification Systems for soil parameters. Please find the
documents for this contextual focus and give a table that I can copy,
listing these documents, with for each of them, a URL link to download
them."* We recorded the document title and the URL link in a dataset for
further analysis.

## 2.2. Data extraction

### 2.2.1. Inclusion rules

To be included in the study, the collected articles and websites should
at least, indicate one of the required information for each step of the
MRV procedure i.e. one information for monitoring, one for reporting and
one for verification. For example, if only information about monitoring
was given, such as the assessed soil parameters, and no information
about reporting nor verification, the document was excluded from the
analysis. Moreover, the MRV procedure was required to include at least
one soil parameter. For example, MRV procedures about greenhouse gas
emissions in forest, focusing on parameters related to the vegetation,
without considering a single soil parameter, were excluded.

### 2.2.2. Duplicate management

The same document or the same MRV procedure could be collected several
times. For example, several scientific articles could include the same
MRV procedure, or a website could appear several times. We considered
any new mention of an already mentioned MRV procedure as duplicate.
Thus, we avoided counting twice the same MRV procedure.

### 2.2.3. Data collection

We considered the land uses and land covers were the MRV procedures are
applied, the geographical scale ( i.e. local such as a field, a farm or
a forest area, regional corresponding to several sites or farms,
national, continental and global scale). We categorized occupations of
stakeholders implementing the MRV procedures as farmers, foresters and
forester associations, public administrators, educational and research
institutions, NGOs, agroindustry, forestry companies, consultants and
others (Chowdhury et al., 2023; Eggers et al., 2020; Pachón Maldonado et
al., 2024; Strauss et al., 2023; Vanino et al., 2023). We indicated the
purpose of the MRV procedure i.e.the reason why it was developed : 1)
voluntary carbon market i.e. a carbon market in which members are not
legally compelled to reduce their emissions but do so voluntarily, 2)
compliance carbon markets also known as mandatory markets, governed by
national, regional, or provincial law and 3) certification i.e.a
procedure to attribute a label (Batjes et al., 2024; Ceschia et al.,
2025). We recorded the actions that were implemented.

Monitoring methodologies were divided in : 1) information about land
management, 2) spatial images, 3) on-site images with photos, 4) soil
samples and 5) modelling (Batjes et al., 2024). In the case of soil
samples, we collected information about the sampling design: 1) the plot
area and 2) the monitoring frequency i.e. duration between two
monitoring sessions (less than every 5 years, between 5 and 10 years,
between 10 and 15 years or more than 15 years as in Batjes et al. 2024).
Soil parameters required in each MRV procedures were listed. We also
recorded if sampling and/or analytical methods comply to existing
standards (e.g. ISO). We described the format of the report (classical
document or online platform, Andries et al. 2021) and the statistical
methodology employed to compute the uncertainty of the results: 1)
probabilistic methods corresponding to Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)
and Bayesian inference, 2) sensitivity analysis, i.e.the effect of the
explanatory variables on the uncertainty of the results and 3) quantile
distribution, with the representation and/or consideration of the
quantiles in the result interpretation (Ceschia et al., 2025). We
recorded the methodology used to compute the reference values : 1) fixed
value, 2) reference value, 3) data distribution, or 4) relative change
(Matson et al. 2024) Regarding verification, five information were
listed : the scheme i.e. action-based or result-based (Batjes et al.
2024), the methodology i.e. soil sampling, satellite data, phone
application or site inspection, its automatization, the auditor
independance and the data access (Batjes et al., 2024). Finally, we
recorded if the MRV procedure was already implemented or under
development and the country where the MRV procedure was implemented or
tested.

### 2.3.1. Management of missing information

Once the data collection was completed, we noticed a large part of
missing information. As missing information could bias the results, in
particular with categorical variables, we decided to keep only variables
that presented more than 70% MRV procedures with information in the
analysis.

### 2.3.2. Description and typology of MRV procedures

We pooled the data collected from the three search methods. We used the
software R 4.3.0 for data analysis building the figures. We designed
with the package ggplot2 (Wickham et al., 2016) bar plots for each
variable and a co-occurrence matrix between stakeholder' and MRV
procedure' s characteristics.

We implemented multiple component analysis (MCA, function MCA, package R
FactomineR, Lê et al., 2008) and a Hierarchical Clustering on Principle
Components (HCPC, function HCPC, package FactoMineR) to identify the
groups of MRV procedures and the particular elements characterizing
them. We computed a v-test and its p-value (Husson et al., 2017). We
focused our analysis on the categories with 1) v-test\>2 and 2) a
p-value\<0.05 (Husson et al., 2017).

### 2.3.3. Building the decision tool

We built a user-friendly interface to access our dataset, with Python
1.29 with the package Streamlit (<https://streamlit.io>) . The outputs
are the MRV procedures with a playing card format, fitted to the context
of the user. All the codes and datasets needed to run the decision tool
are available (See Code and data availability).

```{r Dataset total, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
db_publications<-rbind(db_articles,db_webscraping,db_AI)

  x <- as.character(x)
  x[is.na(x)] <- "Missing_information"
  factor(x)
})

db_publications$Format_Document[db_publications$Format_Document=="NA "]<-"Missing_information"
db_publications$Format_Document<-droplevels(db_publications$Format_Document)
db_publications<- droplevels(db_publications)
```

```{r number MRV procedures, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
#nrow(db_publications)
```

All sources pooled, nine scientific articles and 32 websites were
selected (of 28 articles collected and 1211 websites screened, see Code
and data availability). In total, we found 96 MRV procedures. Only
little information was provided in the documents we collected (Appendix
2). We removed from the analysis, variables with information missing for
more than 30% of the MRV procedures : 1) regarding the monitoring,
sampling frequency, standard methodologies, cost and plot area, 2)
regarding the reporting, uncertainty measurement and threshold
methodology, 3) considering the verification, methodology,
automatization, auditor type and data sharing.

MRV procedures mainly took place in America, Oceania and Europe. Only
few countries were covered in Africa and Asia (Fig.1).

```{r, Map occurrence All, echo=FALSE, include=TRUE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4, dpi=300, out.width="100%", warning=FALSE, , message=FALSE}

tidyr::separate_rows(Country, sep = "_")
df_long <- df_long %>%  mutate(Country = trimws(Country))
country_counts <- df_long %>%  dplyr::count(Country)
world <- ne_countries(returnclass = "sf")

country_counts <- country_counts %>%  mutate(Country = case_when(    Country == "USA" ~ "United States of America",    Country == "UK"  ~ "United Kingdom",    TRUE ~ Country  ))

world_data <- world %>%
left_join(country_counts, by = c("name" = "Country"))

world_data$n[is.na(world_data$n)] <- 0

g_map<- ggplot(world_data) +  
  geom_sf(aes(fill = n)) +  
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +  # gradient one color
  labs(fill = "Number of MRV procedures") +  
  theme_minimal()+
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "#CC3333", labels = label_number(accuracy = 1))+
  theme(
    legend.key.height = unit(0.5, "cm"),

    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),

  theme(text = element_text(family = "save"))

g_map

)
```

**Figure 1. Map of the number of MRV procedures taking place in each
country**

More than 80% of the MRV procedures were already implemented, leaving
the remaining 20% as purely conceptual procedures (Appendix 3).

## 3.1. Data description

Seventy-nine MRV procedures took place in agricultural areas (Fig. 2
a.). The other land uses and land covers were forests (22), peatlands or
wetlands (9) and degraded lands (1, Fig. 2 a.).

MRV procedures took place mainly at local scale (62 MRV procedures) and
then at regional scale (45) and national scale (18, Fig. 6). Only two
MRV procedures was applied at continental or at global scale.

A large diversity of occupations were involved in the MRV procedures.
The majority targeted farmers (59 MRV procedures) and then consultants
(40). At a lesser extend, MRV procedures also included other occupations
as public administrators (25), agroindustry (19), NGO (16), academia
(15), project developers (12), foresters (11), forest companies (3),
software developers (1) and other companies (5, Fig. 2 d.).

Five purposes were found: voluntary and compliance carbon markets,
certification and sustainability measures (Fig. 2 c.).

The main purpose of the MRV procedure was by far, voluntary carbon
market with 84 MRV procedures with 84 MRV procedures.

The main actions were related to the change in agricultural practices
(59 MRV procedures). They could be specified as mineral weathering,
irrigation, grazing practices and biochar application. We found other
very rare actions (less than five MRV procedures) as: afforestation and
reforestation, restoration measures, deforestation, rewetting of
peatlands and wetlands, forest management, fire management and land
conversion (Fig. 2 e.).

**Figure 2. Frequency of MRV procedures according to stakeholders'
characteristics: land uses and land covers (a.), geographical scales
(b.), occupation (c.), purpose (d.) and the implemented actions (e.)**

Regarding monitoring, a total of 22 soil parameters were identified in
the MRV procedures (Fig. 3 a.). Physical, chemical and biological
parameters were assessed. The most frequent was soil organic matter and
carbon, monitored in almost all of them (93 MRV procedures, Fig. 3 a.).
In average, two parameters were assessed by MRV procedure. The minimum
number was one parameter, and the maximum was nine for the procedure MRV
WE020 (measurements include pH, soil organic matter and carbon, texture,
bulk density, nutrient availability, green house gases, soil type,
calcium carbonates, electrical conductivity and water holding capacity,
see Code and data availability).

The most frequent monitoring methodology was modelling with 75 MRV
procedures. Soil samples, spatial images and management information are
also used in more than 50 MRV procedures. We also found a MRV procedure
(MRV WE011) based on site images taken with a smart phone (see Code and
data availability).

```{r Figure Monitoring - Data methodology, echo=FALSE, dpi=300}
# Reshape data from wide to long format
db_data <- db_publications%>%
pivot_longer(cols = c( 
"Data_Land_Management", 
"Data_Spatial_images", 
"Data_Soil_samples", 
"Data_Modelling", 
"Data_on_site_images"), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Response")

# Set factor with desired order
db_data$Response <- factor(db_data$Response, levels = c( "No", "Yes"))
db_data$Variable <- factor(db_data$Variable, levels = c("Data_Land_Management", 
"Data_Spatial_images", 
"Data_Soil_samples", 
"Data_Modelling", 
"Data_on_site_images"))

# Summarize counts by variable and response
summary_counts <- db_data %>%
  group_by(Variable, Response) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(Count = n(), .groups = 'drop')%>%
  complete(Variable, Response, fill = list(Count = 0))

summary_counts2<-subset(summary_counts, Response=="Yes")

# Plot grouped bar chart
g_data<- ggplot(summary_counts2, aes(x = reorder (Variable, Count), y = Count)) +
geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = position_dodge(), fill ="lightcoral", col="#eb5252",width=0.5 )+
labs(
  y = "Number of MRV procedures", 
  x = NULL,
  title="Data collection") +
theme_minimal() +
theme(
  axis.text = element_text(size=14), 
  axis.title = element_text(size=14), 
  plot.title= element_text(size = 14, face = "bold", hjust = 0, margin = margin(b = 8)))+
geom_text(aes(label = Count), position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), hjust=-0.5, size=4)+
scale_y_continuous(
  limits = c(0, 100),
    breaks = seq(0,100, by=20),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0)))+ 
scale_x_discrete(labels = c(
"Data_Land_Management"= "Management information", 
"Data_Spatial_images"="Spatial images", 
"Data_Soil_samples"="Soil samples", 
"Data_Modelling"="Modelling",
"Data_on_site_images" = "Site images"))+  
coord_flip(clip="off")+
  theme(text = element_text(family = "Arial"))
```

Results were for 52 MRV procedures gathered in a classical report. An
online platform was used for 29 MRV of them (Fig. 4 a.).The verification
was mainly based on the results (61 MRV procedures) and on the
implementation of the actions for 20 MRV procedures (Fig. 4 b.).

**Figure 4. Number of MRV procedures according to the reporting format

## 3.2. Co-occurrence between stakeholders' and MRV procedures' characteristics

We looked more precisely at the link between the characteristics of the
stakeholders and the MRV procedures, by focusing on the main
co-occurrences between stakeholders' and MRV procedures' characteristics
(i.e. more than 25 MRV procedures, Fig. 5).

In agricultural areas, organic matter and carbon was the only soil
parameter included in more than 25 MRV procedures. All monitoring
methodologies were very frequent, except on-site images. Both ways of
result reporting were used in more than 25 MRV procedures. Verification
was result-based for more than 25 MRV procedures.

At both local and regional scale, we noticed the same pattern for the
monitoring i.e. focused on soil organic matter and carbon, using a
diversity of methodologies. Results were gathered in a classical report
and the verification was result-based. For more than 25 MRV procedures,
consultants monitored soil organic matter and carbon with modelling,
using result-based verification.

Concerning farmers, they also focused on soil organic matter and carbon,
without any preference for the methodology (except site images). Results
were gathered in a classical report and the verification was
result-based. As expected, regarding the voluntary carbon market, more
than 25 MRV procedures included soil organic matter and carbon. More
than 50 were based on soil sampling and modelling and more than 25 on
land management information or spatial images. Logically, when this
implemented action was the change in agricultural practices, MRV
procedures' characteristics were the same as for farmers.

At a larger picture, a lot of combination stakeholders x MRV procedures
did not exist or were not communicated yet.

**Figure 5. Co-occurrence between the characteristics of stakeholders
and MRV procedures**

## 3.3. Typology of stakeholders and MRV procedures

We classified the MRV procedures into six groups and highlighted their
particular characteristics (Fig. 6).

Group 1, including two MRV procedures, was only characterized by missing
information for stakeholder occupation (Fig. 6 a.). Group 2 included ten
MRV procedures. It stood out from the other groups by covering local
(all the MRV procedures), national (7),continental (2) and global (2)
scales and five occupation types that are public administrators (7),
academia (7), NGOs (7), agroindustry (7) and consultancy (8, Fig. 6 a.).
This group was focused on the change in agricultural practices (9 MRV
procedures, Fig. 6 a.). Another particularity was that, for a part of
the MRV procedures, pH (8 MRV procedures), cationic exchange capacity
(CEC, 3) soil moisture (6), water holding capacity (2), soil type (2),
soil depth (4), nutrients (7), porosity (2), texture (3) and temperature
(2) were monitored (Fig. 6 b.).

Group 3 was also very small with three MRV procedures (Fig.6). Its
particularity was the absence of information regarding the geographical
scale the MRV procedures took place and the presence of a MRV procedure
assessing the impact of the change in grazing rate (Fig. 6 a.).

The largest group was the fourth with 56 MRV procedures (Fig. 6). It was
characterized by a high specificity : the particularities were the
implementation at local scale (for 42 MRV procedures) and nor at
national, continental neither at global scale (almost all the MRV
procedures are not implemented at those scales, Fig. 6 a.). Another
particularity was that these MRV procedures did not take place in
peatlands or wetlands (55 MRV procedures). This group stand out by
targeting farmers (45 MRV procedures) and not consultancy (42).
Regarding implemented actions it was also focused on the change in
agricultural practices (44). The absence of rarer actions were also
group 4's particularities. Regarding monitoring, a particularity was
that almost all the MRV procedures did not include pH (56), moisture
(54), soil depth (53) nor nutrient (55, Fig. 6 b.). Different
methodologies appeared as group 4's particularities : soil sampling,
spatial images and land management information (Fig. 6 b.). The use of
online platform (for 22 MRV procedures) and not a classical report (22)
to display the results was also a particularities of the group (Fig. 6
c.). The last one was that the verification was result-based (43) and
not action-based (37, Fig. 6 c.).

Group 5 included only six MRV procedures (Fig. 6). Most of them focused
on peatlands and wetlands (5 MRV procedures) and excluded agricultural
areas (4), targeting project developers (4) for land restoration (3) and
not change in agricultural practices (4, Fig. 6 a.). Another
particularity was the monitoring of rare soil parameters that are
subsidence (2) and soil depth (4, Fig. 6 b.). This group was also
defined by missing information regarding monitoring methodology (Fig. 6
b.) and verification scheme (Fig. 6 c.).

The sixth group, with 19 MRV procedure was the second largest group. One
of its particularities is to include 13 MRV procedures not taking place
at local scale (Fig. 6 a.). It is also targeting consultancy (for all
the MRV procedures) and not farmers (17), academia (all), NGOs (all) nor
the agroindustry (18, Fig 6 a.). The implemented actions are not known
for all of them (Fig. 6 a.). Regarding monitoring, bulk density was
never assessed and the methodology was always modelling (Fig. 6 b.). The
absence of soil sampling nor land management information was also a
particularity of the group (Fig. 6 b.). It was also characterized by the
absence of information regarding reporting format for 18 MRV procedures
(Fig. 6 c.). Regarding verification, it was action-based (9) and not
result-based (10).

```{r  MCA and HCPC, echo=FALSE,include=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, dpi=300,out.width="100%"}
# Extract HCPC category results

# Build data frame and remove rownames
df_cattot <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(cat_listtot), function(i) {
data.frame(
       cluster = i,
        category = rownames(cat_listtot[[i]]),
         cat_listtot[[i]],
       row.names = NULL
     )
 }))

# Keep only categories with v.test > 2
df_sigtot <- df_cattot[df_cattot$v.test > 2, ]

# Order by cluster and v.test (descending)
df_sigtot <- df_sigtot[order(df_sigtot$cluster, -df_sigtot$v.test), ]

# Reset rownames (clean output)
rownames(df_sigtot) <- NULL
 
# Final table
#df_sigtot[, c("cluster", "category","p.value","v.test")]

df_sigtot2<-subset(df_sigtot, p.value<0.051&v.test>2)
```

```{r Total dataset -  Clusters MRV, echo=FALSE,include=T,fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
# Total Dataset
df_longtot<-rbind(df_long1,df_long2,df_long3,df_long4,df_long5,df_long6)

# Assessing Percentage
df_long_count<- df_longtot%>%
dplyr::count(Cluster, Variable, Value)
df_long_count$Ntot<-NA
df_long_count$Ntot[df_long_count$Cluster=="1"]<-nrow(db1)
df_long_count$Ntot[df_long_count$Cluster=="2"]<-nrow(db2)
df_long_count$Ntot[df_long_count$Cluster=="3"]<-nrow(db3)
df_long_count$Ntot[df_long_count$Cluster=="4"]<-nrow(db4)
df_long_count$Ntot[df_long_count$Cluster=="5"]<-nrow(db5)
df_long_count$Ntot[df_long_count$Cluster=="6"]<-nrow(db6)
df_long_count$Percentage<-df_long_count$n*100/df_long_count$Ntot

df_long_count$Value<-as.factor(df_long_count$Value)
#df_long_count$Value[df_long_count$Value=="Management_practices"|df_long_count$Value=="no"|df_long_count$Value=="No "]<-"No"

# Adding Variable names

# Actions
```

```{r Figure Clusters - Stakeholders, echo=FALSE,include=T, fig.width=20, dpi=300, fig.height=18,out.width="100%", warning=FALSE}
df_long_count_Stakeholders<-subset(df_long_count,Characteristics=="Scale"|Characteristics=="Land_use"|Characteristics=="Occupation"|Characteristics=="Actions"|Characteristics=="Purposes")

# Figure
g_Clusters_Stakeholders<-ggplot(df_long_count_Stakeholders,
       aes(x = Variable, y = Percentage, fill = Value, colour=Particularity, linewidth = Particularity)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Particularity" = "blue")) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c("Particularity" = 2))+
  
  geom_col(width = 0.5) +
  
  ggh4x::facet_nested(
    rows = vars(Characteristics),
    cols = vars(Cluster),
    scales = "free_y",
    strip = strip_themed(
    background_x = elem_list_rect(fill = "#f0ebe2"),
    text_x = elem_list_text(face = "bold")),
    switch = "y",
    space = "free_y",
    
     labeller = labeller(
    Characteristics = c(
      "Actions" = "Actions",
      "Land_use" = "Land use",
      "Monitoring_data"="Data",
      "Occupation"="Occupation",
      "Parameters"="Parameters",
      "Purposes"="Purposes",
      "Reporting_format"="Format",
      "Scale"="Scale",
      "Verification_scheme"="Scheme"),
    Cluster = c(
      "1" = "Group 1 (N=2)",
      "2" = "Group 2 (N=10)",
      "3" = "Group 3 (N=3)",
      "4" = "Group 4 (N=56)",
      "5" = "Group 5 (N=6)",
      "6" = "Group 6 (N=19)")))+
  
  theme(strip.placement = "outside", 
        strip.switch.pad.grid = unit(0.1, "cm"),
        legend.position = "bottom",
        axis.text.x  = element_text(size = 14),  # x labels
        axis.text.y  = element_text(size = 14),  # y labels
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 14),  # x-axis title
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 14),# y-axis title
        strip.text = element_text(size = 14), # facets
        legend.text = element_text(size = 14),   # legend labels
        legend.title = element_text(size = 14))+  # legend title  
  coord_flip()+
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = 0.6, vjust = 0.25,position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), color = "black", size = 5,fontface="bold") +
 scale_x_discrete(
  labels = c(
"Scale_Local"="Local", 
"Scale_Regional"="Regional",
"Scale_National"="National",                               
"Scale_Continental"="Continental",
"Scale_Global"="Global",

# Landuse
"Land_use_Agriculture"="Agriculture",
"Land_use_Forest"="Forest",
"Land_use_Degraded_land"="Degraded land",
"Land_use_Peatland_Wetland"="Peatland and wetlands",    
  
# Occupation
"Occupation_Farmers"="Farmers", 
"Occupation_Public_Administrators"="Public administrators",    
"Occupation_Educational_Institutions_Research"="Academia",
"Occupation_NGOs"="NGOs", 
"Occupation_Agroindustry"="Agroindustry",
"Occupation_Consultancy"="Consultancy",
"Occupation_Project_developer"="Project developer",
"Occupation_Other_companies"="Other companies",   
"Occupation_Software_developers"="Software developers",

# Purposes
"Certification"="Certification",
"Compliance_carbon_market"="Compliance carbon market",
"Decision_making"="Decision making",
"Sustainability"="Sustainability",
"Voluntary_carbon_market"="Voluntary carbon market",

# Drivers
"Driver_Agricultural_practices"="Agricultural practices",                
"Driver_Conservation"="Conservation measures",
"Driver_Restoration"="Restoration measures",
"Driver_Weathering"="Weathering",                    
"Driver_Grazing"="Grazing",
"Driver_Irrigation"="Irrigation",
"Driver_Land_conversion"="Land conversion",
"Driver_Afforestation_Reforestation"="Af-Reforestation",
"Driver_Forest_management"="Forest management",
"Driver_Deforestation"="Deforestation",
"Driver_Fire_management"="Fire management"))+
  
scale_fill_manual(
  values = c(
    "Yes" = "#CC9D00",
    "No" = "#FFD300", 
    "Missing_information" = "light grey"),
  labels= c(
  "Yes" = "Presence",
  "No" = "Absence",
  "Missing_information" = "Missing information")) 
g_Clusters_Stakeholders
```

c.  Reporting and Verification characteristics

**Figure 6. Number of MRV procedures per category in each group and of
MRV procedures per category in each group and groups' particularities**

## 3.4. Decision tool

To encourage knowledge transfer between scientists and non-scientists,
we developed a decision tool to help users in the choice of an adapted
MRV procedure for soil health. It is available online:
<https://mrv-procedures-soil-health.streamlit.app/>. We used the playing
card format to summarize the collected information. The welcome page
explains the purpose of the tool and the information presented on each
MRV card. Then, the user selects its context\`s characteristics and the
tool provide the MRV procedures with a level of similarity higher than
80%. The MRV procedures are presented with the format of cards.

The first page of the decision tool corresponds to the user (i.e. the
stakeholder)'s characteristics : 1) On which land use do you want to
apply the MRV procedure?, 2) At which geographical scale do you want to
apply the MRV procedure?, 3) What is the purpose of the MRV procedure?,
4) Which type of actions do you want to implement? and 5)What is your
occupation? After answering the previous questions, the MRV cards
corresponding to these criteria are suggested. The tool will present all
the MRV cards with a percentage of similarity as the number of items
fitted with user' wishes divided by the total number of items.

# 4. Discussion

With only nine scientific articles included in our literature review,
the term MRV seems to be rarely used by soil scientists. A large part of
scientific articles when mentioning MRV only focus on the monitoring
part. The term MRV is more common in the private sector as shown by the
higher number of MRV procedures coming from company websites, collected
with web scraping. Our study illustrates the difference in terminology
between academia and the private sector. These differences can lead to
communication difficulties (Weninger et al., 2024). However, scientists
implement MRV procedures without calling them like this: they monitor
soils, verify their data and report the results in the form of
scientific articles. National soil monitoring networks are good examples
of these "hidden" MRV procedures (Imbert et al., 2024).

Major characteristics of MRV procedures were discarded from the analysis
due to lack of information. We are missing knowledge on: sampling
designs (plot area, sampling frequency), costs, uncertainty reporting,
verification provider and data sharing or availability. A recent study
in Wallonia, Belgium tried to develop a cost model for three MRV systems
namely decision support tools, process-based models, and direct soil
measurements. They suggest that their generic cost model development can
be extrapolated across various context to estimate MRV costs of carbon
farming (Vanderheyden et al. 2026). Again, we encourage the providers of
MRV procedures to clearly communicate about those later points to avoid
suspicion of green washing.

In our study, very few MRV procedures took place in Africa or in Asia.
This result was surprising because compensation using carbon credits by
reforestation mainly takes place in the countries of the Global South
i.e. Africa, Asia, Oceania (Australia and New Zealand excluded) and
Latin America (Cheong, 2025). Possible explanations would be that the
term MRV is not used by all the actors of the private sector or that
these MRV procedures do not include soil parameters. Thus, this might be
a limitation of our study.

The majority of the MRV procedures involved farmers willing to get
involved in the voluntary carbon market, by changing their agricultural
practices. In this way, our study illustrates the dominance of the
voluntary carbon market in the MRV context. In parallel to carbon
markets, certain MRV procedures were designed to help stakeholders in
decision making (MRV WE019 and MRV WE040). The aim of these MRV
procedures is to give indications to farmers to improve farm management.
The farmer chooses to spend money on soil monitoring and compensate this
investment with better management (more efficient use of intrants
mainly).

Organic matter and carbon was the soil parameter the most frequently
monitored. The next step is to understand how to pass from a (mainly)
carbon-focused MRV procedure to a broader one, assessing soil health.
Several strategies are used to assess soil health but they can give
contradictory results (Zwaan et al., 2026). A recent study, based on
expert knowledge, advised the monitoring of around thirty parameters,
related to soil, topography and climate to accurately assess soil health
(Vazquez, et al., 2025). Thus, with a maximum of nine parameters
assessed, existing MRV procedures do not currently cover soil health.

Regarding monitoring methodology, there is a trade-off between costs and
accuracy (Ihasusta et al., 2026). In general, soil sampling is more
accurate than modelling (Batjes et al., 2024). However, modelling is
more frequently used because it is faster and cheaper to implement.
Empirical or process-based modelling is associated with soil sampling
that is called a "measure-remeasure model" approach to calibrate and
validate the model. Soil sampling could also be used alone in a "measure
and re-measure" approach, and based on values from other locations and
specific sampling design.

Surprisingly, verification was more often result-based than
action-based. We could think that action-based would be the most
frequent, as it requires only a simple, rapid field visit to check
management changes, far more cheaper than result based, requiring a new
soil assessment including sampling and measurement. As requiring a
second monitoring session, result-based verification is more accurate
than action-based.

To synthesize our results, we built a typology of soil MRV procedures
(Fig. 7).

```{r Figure Cards - Typology MRV procedures, echo=FALSE, fig.width=12, fig.height=10, fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("Figure_7_typology_cards.png")
```

**Figure 7. Typology of soil MRV procedures**

We classified them into six groups including from two to 56 MRV
procedures. Group 1 was only characterized by the lack of information
and thus reflected the main limitation of our study. The five other
groups addressed different stakeholders. Four of them targeted
stakeholders of the agricultural sector: farmers (group 4) specifically
breeders (with changes in grazing rate for the group 3), consultants
(group 6) or rarer and more diversified stakeholders (i.e. scientist,
agroindustry, public administration and NGOs for the group 2). The last
one (group 5) targeted project developers for peatlands and wetland
restoration. The two largest groups (group 4 and 6) demonstrated
different strategies: more accurate monitoring and verification
methodologies for group 4, cheaper ones for group 6. Group 6 was
characterized by the fact that the bulk density was not assessed even if
it is an essential information to be able to compute soil carbon stocks
(Martin et al., 2009). So, again, we encourage a strong partnership
between MRV providers and scientists for developing accurate soil health
MRV procedures. This type of co-creation of MRV procedures for soil
health is currently on going (Imbert et al., 2024).

# 5. Conclusions

This study sheds light upon an overview of MRV procedures for soils. It
bridges the scientific gap, previously completed by studies focused on
the most common applications, i.e. carbon markets in the agricultural
context (Batjes et al., 2024). In the soil science community, MRV is an
emergent framework, and we strongly encourage soil scientists to employ
the term MRV more stringently in their publications to engage in
communication with the private sector. Aligning the scientific language
to common market terminology will also help to improve the robustness of
proprietary MRV procedures, as developers and users can more easily
refer to scientific research that critically reflects such developments.
We also encourage the providers of MRV procedures to clearly communicate
to avoid suspicion of green washing. Indeed, major information as
sampling design or costs were often inaccessible or scarce. Therefore,
more visibility of these components of MRV procedures is required. In
the present study, we succeeded in building a typology of MRV procedures
and to develop a decision tool to make our work more easily accessible
to as many people as possible. The next step is to understand how to
pass from a (mainly) carbon-focused MRV procedure to a broader one,
assessing soil health. With a maximum of nine parameters assessed,
existing MRV procedures do not currently cover soil health. They could
be completed with new soil parameters, but the major problem stays the
cost.

```{r PRISMA - Figures, echo=FALSE, include=T, fig.width=6, dpi=600}
add_label_above <- function(img, mytags, mytitles) {
  mylabels <- paste0(mytags, ". ", mytitles)
  w <- image_info(img)$width
  label_img <- image_blank(width = w, height = 70, color = "white") |>
    image_annotate(mylabels, size = 16, gravity = "west", location = "+20+0",
                    color = "black", weight = 700)
  image_append(image_join(list(label_img, img)), stack = TRUE)
}

imgs_labeled <- Map(add_label_above, imgs, mytags, mytitles)
PRISMA_combined <- image_append(image_join(imgs_labeled), stack = TRUE)

image_write(PRISMA_combined, path = "Appendix_1_PRISMA.png")
knitr::include_graphics("prisma_combined.png")
```

## Appendix C. Number (percentage) of MRV procedures according the implementation level

```{r, Implementation All, echo=FALSE, include=TRUE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, dpi=300}

db_Implementation<-table(db_publications$Implementation)

db_Implementation2<-as.data.frame(db_Implementation)
names(db_Implementation2)<-c("Implementation", "Number")

db_Implementation2$Percent <- db_Implementation2$Number / sum(db_Implementation2$Number) * 100
db_Implementation2$Label <- paste0(db_Implementation2$Number, " (", round(db_Implementation2$Percent, 1), "%)")

g_Implementation<-ggplot(db_Implementation2, aes(x = "", y = Number, fill = Implementation)) +
geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1, col="black") +
coord_polar(theta = "y") +
geom_text(aes(label = Label), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5)) +  # place labels in the middle of each slice
scale_fill_manual(
values = c("Implemented" = "aquamarine3", "Project"="orange", "Missing_information"="lightgrey"),
labels = c( "Implemented", "Missing information", "Project"))+
theme_void()

g_Implementation

ggsave(
  filename = "Appendix_3_description_implementation.png", 
  plot = g_Implementation, 
  width = 8,
  height = 4,
  dpi = 300,
  units = "in",
  bg="white"
)
```
